title: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia
summary: Use the 4Ts score before ordering HIT tests. For intermediate or high probability, stop all heparin, begin nonheparin anticoagulation, obtain an IgG-specific PF4/heparin immunoassay, and use a functional platelet-activation assay to resolve positive or discordant results.
seoDescription: Clinical approach to HIT testing and anticoagulation: 4Ts-guided testing, PF4/heparin assay interpretation, functional confirmation, and nonheparin therapy.
clinicalQuestion: How should clinicians use 4Ts scoring, PF4/heparin testing, functional assays, and nonheparin anticoagulation in suspected HIT?
keyTakeaways: Do not send HIT antibody testing solely for thrombocytopenia during heparin exposure; first estimate pretest probability with the 4Ts score. A low score can exclude HIT in many patients, whereas intermediate or high probability warrants immunoassay testing. [11][19][23]
In suspected acute HIT with a 4Ts score of at least 4, stop heparin and initiate a nonheparin anticoagulant while diagnostic testing proceeds. [11][12]

A positive PF4/heparin immunoassay does not establish HIT because many detected antibodies do not activate platelets; confirm clinically consequential antibodies with a functional assay when available. [13][19][24]

Interpret PF4/heparin ELISA optical density with the clinical probability: higher optical density is associated with serotonin-release assay positivity and thrombosis risk, while weak-positive results generate substantial overtreatment. [7][21]
Fondaparinux is used off label for suspected acute HIT; argatroban is problematic in impaired hepatic function and aPTT confounding can complicate monitoring in consumptive coagulopathy. [9]

sections.heading: Identify the platelet pattern that warrants a HIT workup
sections.intro: Anchor testing to timing, platelet trajectory, thrombosis, and competing explanations.
paragraphs: Suspect immune HIT when thrombocytopenia develops after unfractionated or low-molecular-weight heparin exposure, particularly with a platelet fall beginning around day 4 or 5 of exposure, new thrombosis, or both. HIT is driven by platelet-activating antibodies to PF4-heparin complexes and is a prothrombotic—not bleeding-predominant—drug reaction. [11][14]

Calculate the 4Ts score before ordering laboratory testing. Its four elements are the relative platelet-count fall, timing of decline, thrombosis or other sequelae, and the presence of alternative causes of thrombocytopenia. A score below 4 should generally redirect evaluation toward non-HIT causes rather than trigger routine HIT immunoassay testing; a score of 4 or greater should trigger prompt HIT-directed testing and management. [12][19][20][23]

Reassess alternative explanations explicitly before labeling HIT: in dialysis-associated thrombocytopenia, the differential includes infection, pseudothrombocytopenia, antiphospholipid syndrome, implicated drugs, and dialyzer membrane or sterilization effects. In cardiac surgery, PF4-heparin antibodies are frequent: approximately 50% of about 950 patients developed antibodies within 30 days by polyspecific ELISA, without an associated increase in death or thromboembolism. Testing in that setting should therefore be limited to patients with an appropriately high clinical probability. [12][22]
bullets: Document the baseline platelet count and calculate the percentage fall; the dialysis-focused algorithm flags a fall greater than 50% or a platelet count below 100 × 10^9/L as a thrombocytopenic pattern requiring assessment in the right clinical context. [12]
Ask specifically about new venous or arterial thrombosis, including dialysis-access thrombosis; HIT-associated thrombosis can be extensive and may lead to limb loss or death. [23]
Do not use a positive antibody result to override a low-probability clinical presentation without resolving discordance. [13][19][22]

table.caption: 4Ts-directed first actions in suspected HIT. [11][12][19][23]
rows: Low 4Ts score (<4)
Do not routinely order HIT immunoassay; investigate alternative causes of thrombocytopenia. [12]
Do not institute HIT-directed nonheparin anticoagulation solely for HIT suspicion. [12]
Intermediate or high 4Ts score (≥4)
Order a PF4/heparin immunoassay; if positive, obtain a functional platelet-activation assay to confirm clinically significant antibodies. [11][19][23]
Stop heparin and begin a nonheparin anticoagulant while results are pending. [11][12]

sections.heading: Order and interpret PF4/heparin immunoassays in clinical context
sections.intro: Immunoassays are screening tests; they are sensitive but not intrinsically diagnostic.
paragraphs: For intermediate- or high-probability HIT, obtain a validated PF4/heparin antibody immunoassay, preferably an assay restricted to IgG antibodies. British guidance recommends that initial ELISAs have sensitivity greater than 95% and detect IgG only; a negative high-sensitivity ELISA can exclude HIT. [22]

A positive PF4/heparin assay identifies antibodies but not necessarily pathogenic platelet activation. Many immunoassays detect non-platelet-activating IgG as well as IgM and IgA antibodies, which limits their clinical specificity and positive predictive value. Interpret a positive result jointly with the 4Ts score, platelet course, thrombotic phenotype, and—when available—a functional assay. [13][19][22][24]

Use ELISA optical density as a probability modifier rather than a stand-alone treatment threshold. Higher optical density values correlate with serotonin-release assay positivity and thrombosis risk. In one surgical and cardiac ICU cohort, serotonin-release assay positivity occurred in 81.8% of patients with ELISA optical density at least 2.0, compared with 4.5% at 0.85 to 1.99 and 1.0% at 0 to 0.84. [7][21]

Avoid overinterpreting antibody positivity after cardiac surgery or other high-seropositivity settings. A polyspecific ELISA cutoff of optical density 0.4 identified frequent postoperative antibodies without increased thromboembolism or death, illustrating why indiscriminate testing creates false diagnostic signals. [22]
bullets: Negative high-sensitivity IgG PF4/heparin ELISA: exclude HIT and discontinue HIT-directed alternative anticoagulation when the clinical course is concordant. [12][22]
Positive immunoassay plus intermediate/high 4Ts score: continue heparin avoidance and send functional testing to establish whether antibodies activate platelets. [11][19][23]
Positive immunoassay with low 4Ts score or a convincing competing cause: treat as discordant testing, not confirmed HIT; reassess assay type, optical density, and alternative diagnoses. [19][22]

rows: 4Ts <4
Clinical probability is low; the 4Ts score can exclude HIT in many patients when applied by experienced observers. [19][23]
Evaluate other causes; avoid routine HIT testing and unnecessary alternative anticoagulation. [12]
4Ts ≥4; high-sensitivity IgG ELISA negative

4Ts ≥4; immunoassay positive
Antibodies are present, but pathogenic platelet activation remains unproven. [13][19]

Strong ELISA reactivity substantially increases likelihood of SRA positivity in one ICU cohort. [21]
Treat the result as higher-probability HIT while functional confirmation is pursued; integrate with 4Ts and thrombosis status. [7][21]
Positive ELISA with low or intermediate OD
Weak-positive results have lower functional-assay positivity and require careful clinical correlation. [21]
Do not confirm HIT from ELISA alone; prioritize functional testing and competing diagnoses. [13][19][21]

sections.heading: Use functional assays to distinguish pathogenic HIT antibodies
sections.intro: Functional testing is decisive when the clinical and immunoassay data support HIT.
paragraphs: Order a platelet-activation assay after a positive immunoassay in a patient with intermediate or high 4Ts probability. The serotonin-release assay (SRA) and heparin-induced platelet activation assay (HIPA) are established functional approaches; both test whether patient antibody-heparin-PF4 complexes activate donor platelets. [7][11][19][23][24]

Functional assays improve specificity because they identify platelet-activating antibodies rather than antibody binding alone. In SRA, serotonin release from platelet dense granules is measured; in HIPA, washed donor platelets are combined with patient serum and heparin and platelet aggregation is assessed. [7][20][24]

Do not delay acute management in a patient with intermediate or high clinical probability solely because functional testing is available only through specialized laboratories. Functional assays are technically challenging, differ by platelet donor selection, sample preparation, heparin concentration, endpoint, and control interpretation, and are often not rapidly available. [19][23][24]

Treat discordant results as a diagnostic problem rather than a reflex mandate for indefinite HIT labeling. Immunoassay-positive but functional-assay-negative results can occur because detected antibodies are nonactivating; interpretation should return to the 4Ts score, optical density, thrombosis, assay characteristics, and medication effects. Potent P2Y12 inhibition has been reported to yield false-negative SRA results. [8][13][19][20]
bullets: SRA or HIPA positive with compatible clinical presentation: confirm HIT and continue nonheparin anticoagulation. [11][19][20]
Functional assay negative after a positive immunoassay: reconsider HIT, particularly with low clinical probability or weak immunoassay reactivity. [13][19][21]

If P2Y12 receptor inhibition is present, recognize potential false-negative functional testing and integrate strong clinical and immunoassay evidence rather than relying on one assay result in isolation. [6][8]

table.caption: Functional assays used to confirm platelet-activating HIT antibodies. [7][19][20][23][24]
rows: Serotonin-release assay
Heparin-dependent serotonin release from donor platelet dense granules, reflecting platelet activation. [20][24]
Accepted functional reference assay but technically demanding and often unavailable in real time. [19][23][24]
Heparin-induced platelet activation assay
Platelet aggregation after donor washed platelets are exposed to patient serum and heparin. [7][20]
Can provide functional confirmation; assay performance and interpretation depend on laboratory methodology. [20][24]

sections.heading: Stop heparin and anticoagulate suspected acute HIT before confirmation
sections.intro: The treatment decision follows clinical probability because thrombotic risk can be catastrophic.
paragraphs: For a 4Ts score of at least 4, immediately stop unfractionated heparin and low-molecular-weight heparin, send the immunoassay, and start nonheparin anticoagulation while testing proceeds. This approach addresses the prothrombotic interval before laboratory confirmation; heparin avoidance plus nonheparin anticoagulation are the core acute management measures. [11][12]

Argatroban is a direct thrombin inhibitor used for acute HIT, but impaired hepatic function is a major selection constraint. Its monitoring can also be difficult when aPTT is confounded by HIT-associated consumptive coagulopathy. Do not select argatroban without accounting for these limitations. [9]

Fondaparinux has been used off label in suspected acute HIT, including patients with intermediate or high clinical probability. Registry data described it as effective and safe without HIT-specific complications, but randomized trial data were identified as needed and fondaparinux does not carry an acute-HIT indication. Document its off-label status when it is selected. [9]

For hemodialysis-associated suspected HIT, stop heparin and use nonheparin anticoagulation when 4Ts is at least 4. In patients with a history of HIT, danaparoid or citrate are described options for dialysis anticoagulation, although danaparoid has limited access and is not approved in the United States. [9][12]
bullets: Suspected HIT, 4Ts ≥4: discontinue all heparin exposure and begin a nonheparin anticoagulant pending testing. [11][12]
High-sensitivity immunoassay negative: stop the nonheparin anticoagulant and resume heparin if clinically required. [12][22]
Confirmed HIT: maintain heparin avoidance and continue nonheparin anticoagulation; reassess thrombosis status and bleeding risk as treatment is continued. [11][23]
Avoid treating every positive PF4/heparin ELISA as confirmed HIT; unnecessary direct-thrombin-inhibitor exposure carries bleeding risk and has contributed to overtreatment. [13][21]

subsections.heading: Treatment selection limits supported by available data
paragraphs: The available comparative evidence supports a practical selection distinction rather than a universal drug hierarchy: fondaparinux is an off-label option with supportive registry experience, whereas argatroban has a specific hepatic-function limitation and potential aPTT-monitoring interference in consumptive coagulopathy. No dose, renal adjustment, or duration regimen is specified here because those parameters are not established in the cited material. [9]

sections.heading: Prevent overdiagnosis and treatment-related harm
sections.intro: The main preventable error is treating an antibody result rather than a clinicopathologic syndrome.
paragraphs: HIT overdiagnosis is common when clinicians bypass pretest probability assessment. In an ICU study of 135 tested patients, 80 had positive PF4/heparin ELISAs, but only 11 had positive SRA results; 21.5% received argatroban or lepirudin. The discrepancy illustrates the clinical cost of treating ELISA positivity without adequate 4Ts and functional-assay integration. [21]

Use an IgG-specific, high-sensitivity initial ELISA and retain the quantitative optical density in the chart and handoff. A positive result should be interpreted with the clinical estimate of pretest probability; a negative high-sensitivity assay excludes HIT, while a positive assay requires assessment for platelet activation. [7][19][22]

When HIT remains plausible, actively assess for thrombosis rather than relying on the platelet count alone. HIT is associated with extensive venous and arterial thrombosis, limb loss, and death; mortality was 22% in a VITT cohort, but that outcome estimate applies to VITT rather than heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and should not be transferred to HIT. [3][23]

Record the ultimate diagnostic status precisely: suspected HIT, immunoassay-positive/functional assay pending, functional-confirmed HIT, or HIT excluded. This prevents inappropriate long-term heparin avoidance after a low-probability or functionally unconfirmed antibody result. [13][19][22]
bullets: Do not extrapolate VITT testing or risk estimates to HIT: VITT antibodies directly target PF4 and are associated with adenoviral-based vaccines, but this is a distinct anti-PF4 disorder. [1][4]
When thrombocytopenia occurs during dialysis, investigate circuit-, drug-, infection-, and laboratory-related alternatives alongside HIT rather than reflexively assigning heparin causality. [12]

For a positive PF4/heparin test with a negative functional assay, review exposure timing, 4Ts scoring, optical density, thrombosis, and potential P2Y12 inhibitor interference before retaining a HIT diagnosis. [6][8][19][21]

table.caption: Common HIT-testing errors and corrective actions. [12][13][19][21][22]
rows: Ordering ELISA without 4Ts assessment
Antibody detection has limited positive predictive value when pretest probability is low. [19][23]
Calculate 4Ts first; generally avoid testing when score is below 4. [12]
Calling any positive ELISA HIT
Not all anti-PF4/heparin antibodies activate platelets. [13][19]
Use IgG assay characteristics, optical density, clinical probability, and functional testing. [7][21][22]
Continuing empiric alternative anticoagulation after negative high-sensitivity ELISA
A negative high-sensitivity ELISA excludes HIT. [22]
Stop nonheparin anticoagulation and resume heparin if indicated. [12]
Ignoring alternative causes after cardiac surgery or during dialysis
Antibody positivity and thrombocytopenia have multiple non-HIT explanations in these settings. [12][22]
Restrict testing to compatible platelet and thrombosis patterns; investigate competing causes concurrently. [12][22]
